title: Agrius
summary: Agrius is a destructive intrusion set that public reporting links to Iranian state-aligned activity, with targets concentrated in Israel and in organisations connected to it. Analysts describe access obtained through web shells planted on internet-facing servers and through credentials recycled from earlier compromises, followed by deployment of tooling that overwrites or destroys data rather than encrypting it for ransom. That distinction shapes incident response: wipers have been reported to imitate ransomware notes, so a plan built only around decryption and negotiation can waste the hours when containment matters most. Reported activity has also included social engineering of employees through recruitment-themed lures. Evidence typically appears in web server logs, in unexpected scheduled tasks or services, and in file modification patterns that show destruction rather than encryption. Attribution is asserted in public reporting with varying confidence across vendors, and the tooling overlaps with other Iran-linked clusters.

beginner.definition: Agrius is a name for a group of attackers that public reports link to Iran. The group is known for destroying data instead of stealing it. It often hides a small program on a web server to keep a way in. Then it uses that way in to damage the files of a company.
beginner.whyItMatters: Ransomware at least leaves the hope of recovery. Destruction does not. If an attacker overwrites your files, no key exists to unlock them. Many teams practise only for ransomware, so they lose time when the real goal is damage. Agrius reminds us to prepare for attacks that simply want to break things.
howItWorks: The attackers find a flaw in a web server that faces the public internet.
They place a small hidden program there, called a web shell, to return later.
With that access they steal passwords and then move to other computers inside.
When they are ready, they run tools that overwrite files and destroy data.
Sometimes they leave a ransom note, so the attack looks like a robbery for money.
This trick wastes time, because paying money can never bring destroyed data back.
beginner.example: Picture a shop where a thief copies the keys and returns at night. Instead of taking the till, he pours paint over every machine and then leaves a note asking for money to stop. The owner calls a locksmith and waits, because the note looks like a normal robbery. But there is nothing to unlock, and the machines are ruined. A company that only practises for locked doors will not know what to do when the intruder came to smash things.
takeaways: Prepare for data destruction, not only for encrypted files.
Check your web servers for hidden files and unexpected programs.
Keep offline copies of important data that no attacker can overwrite.

objectives: Explain what Agrius is and why public reporting treats it as a destructive cluster.
Describe how a web shell on an internet-facing server supports later internal access.
Explain why a ransom note does not prove that an attack is financially motivated.
Identify the host and server evidence that distinguishes wiping from encryption.
Summarise recovery planning that survives destruction of production data.
Describe how vendor attribution for this cluster differs in stated confidence.
